title: Frontend System Design
summary: A frontend system must stay understandable as users, features, and teams grow.

subtopics.title: Clarify the user task
subtopics.explanation: Start with the person’s goal and the conditions they face. Ask about devices, network quality, data size, privacy, and time expectations. It is like drawing a route only after choosing the destination. These answers shape the design and reveal which constraints deserve priority. For example, for a dashboard, decide whether filters belong in the URL so teammates can share the same view. In a real page, a mobile checkout on a slow connection may need smaller assets and recoverable requests.

subtopics.title: Sketch the page and states
subtopics.explanation: Sketch the main screens and transitions. Include loading, empty, success, error, and permission states. It is like drawing the floor plan and the paths people take through it. Check that keyboard and assistive technology users can complete the same tasks. For example, a slow network may require partial rendering and clear retry states. In a real page, a search result page may store filters in the URL for sharing and browser history.

subtopics.title: Plan data flow
subtopics.explanation: Identify where data comes from, how it is cached, and how stale requests are canceled. Define error shapes and which parts of the screen can load independently. It is like planning plumbing and deciding what happens when one pipe is unavailable. Keep user-visible state consistent with the data source. For example, a private account screen should not send secret credentials in its JavaScript bundle. In a real page, an empty state should explain how to create the first item.

subtopics.title: Choose boundaries
subtopics.explanation: Group components around related behavior and team ownership. Share a component when its behavior is stable, not simply because two screens look similar. It is like designing rooms around real activities. Keep private server logic off the client, where visitors can inspect the code. For example, keyboard users need a complete path through menus, dialogs, and forms. In a real page, a design should state which server owns permission checks and which data may be cached.

subtopics.title: Measure and evolve
subtopics.explanation: Set performance targets, observe errors, and release changes in manageable steps. Design decisions can change as traffic and teams grow. It is like checking a building after people move in and adjusting where needed. Explain why a choice fits current constraints and what evidence would trigger a redesign. For example, observe interaction latency and failed requests after release before changing architecture. In a real page, a release dashboard can track errors and interaction latency against a target.

foundations.overview: Frontend system design is the process of planning how a user-facing application should meet its goals as it grows. It covers screens, data flow, component boundaries, performance, accessibility, and failure states. Think of it like planning a building around the people who will use it. Begin with user tasks and constraints, then explain trade-offs and how the system will be measured.
foundations.whyItMatters: A design discussion should connect architecture choices to user goals and operating constraints. Clear trade-offs make the system easier to implement, measure, and change.
foundations.browserPerspective: A frontend system includes browser code, APIs, delivery infrastructure, and the people who operate it.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Use diagrams to explain screens, data flow, caching, and failure recovery before choosing libraries.
foundations.businessImpact: A clear plan reduces delivery risk and keeps user needs visible as features grow.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Boundaries should reflect behavior, ownership, and privacy.
foundations.performanceImpact: Set performance budgets and observe real-user outcomes after launch.
commonUseCases: Design a responsive dashboard with filters and saved views.
Plan an authenticated form that handles slow requests and server errors.

commonMisconceptions.myth: System design is mainly about choosing a framework
commonMisconceptions.reality: It is about requirements, boundaries, data flow, failure behavior, and tradeoffs.
Scale, team size, privacy, and user needs change the right choices.

commonMisconceptions.myth: System design is choosing a popular frontend framework.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Framework choice is one decision among data flow, UX states, accessibility, security, and operations.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A diagram alone proves a design is production ready.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Explain trade-offs, failure handling, ownership, measurements, and how the design evolves.

keyTakeaways: Start with the person’s goal and the conditions they face.
Sketch the main screens and transitions.
Identify where data comes from, how it is cached, and how stale requests are canceled.
Group components around related behavior and team ownership.
Set performance targets, observe errors, and release changes in manageable steps.
